questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of scanning every cell in an m by n matrix?

options.text: O(m * n), because each cell is examined a constant number of times.
options.explanation: Right. There are m * n total cells, each visited in constant O(1) time.

options.text: O(m + n), because the algorithm only traverses the matrix perimeter.
options.explanation: Scanning all cells visits the interior, not just perimeter borders.

options.text: O((m * n)^2), because nested loops always produce quadratic complexity.
options.explanation: Nested loops over independent dimensions produce O(m * n), not quadratic.

options.text: O(log(m * n)), because matrices support binary search by default.
options.explanation: Unsorted 2D arrays cannot skip elements using binary search.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case auxiliary space complexity of recursive Depth-First Search on an m by n grid?

options.text: O(1), because recursion reuses the same CPU registers without heap allocations.
options.explanation: Every recursive call allocates a stack frame in thread memory.

options.text: O(m * n), because the call stack can grow to the total number of connected cells.
options.explanation: Right. If the entire grid is connected land, call frames reach depth m * n.

options.text: O(m + n), because stack frames pop immediately after visiting each column.
options.explanation: A snaking connected path can traverse all m * n cells before unwinding.

options.text: O(log(m * n)), because grid division halves search space at each branch.
options.explanation: Grid DFS does not halve inputs like a binary divide-and-conquer algorithm.

options.text: Reverse each row first, then reverse every column.
options.explanation: Reversing rows and columns produces a 180-degree rotation, not 90 degrees.

options.text: Invert all cell values and sort each column ascending.
options.explanation: Sorting alters matrix contents rather than rotating coordinates.

options.text: Transpose across the main diagonal, then reverse each row.
options.explanation: Right. Transposing swaps coordinates, and reversing rows turns it clockwise.

options.text: Swap opposing corners and rotate each ring with four pointers.
options.explanation: Corner swapping alone fails to relocate non-corner edge cells.

questions.prompt: Why is marking visited cells essential when running Depth-First Search on a grid?

options.text: It prevents infinite recursion cycles between adjacent neighboring cells.
options.explanation: Right. Without visited marks, recursion bounces back and forth forever.

options.text: It speeds up Swift memory deallocation when stack frames unwind.
options.explanation: Marking visited cells tracks graph state, not memory deallocation.

options.text: It forces LLVM to optimize the search into an iterative while loop.
options.explanation: Marking cell values does not trigger compiler loop transformations.

options.text: It converts the matrix from row-major layout to column-major layout.
options.explanation: Visited marks modify cell values without changing array memory layout.

questions.prompt: Why does traversing a Swift [[Int]] matrix row by row perform faster than column by column?

options.text: Column-by-column iteration requires asynchronous thread locks.
options.explanation: Standard array traversals run synchronously without thread locks.

options.text: Row-by-row iteration accesses contiguous memory buffers, maximizing CPU cache hits.
options.explanation: Right. Each row array occupies contiguous memory, aiding CPU prefetchers.

options.text: Swift arrays store all columns in a single global hash map.
options.explanation: Swift arrays are linear sequential buffers, not global hash maps.

options.text: Row traversal automatically skips default zero values during iteration.
options.explanation: Iteration visits every element sequentially regardless of value.

questions.prompt: Why is Breadth-First Search preferred over Depth-First Search for finding the shortest path in an unweighted grid?

options.text: BFS consumes less auxiliary memory than DFS on large grids.

options.explanation: BFS requires an explicit queue buffer to manage frontier cells.

questions.prompt: Explain why checking matrix.isEmpty is essential before accessing matrix[0].count in Swift, and describe the error that occurs if you omit this check. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, accessing an element by index on an empty array triggers an immediate fatal error because the index is out of bounds. If a matrix has no rows, reading matrix[0].count attempts to access index 0 and crashes the application at runtime. Checking guard !matrix.isEmpty verifies that at least one row exists before inspecting column length. This guard handles edge cases safely.

rubric.criterion: Explains that accessing index 0 on an empty array triggers an out-of-bounds runtime crash.
Identifies that matrix[0].count requires at least one row to exist.
Recommends checking guard !matrix.isEmpty to handle empty edge cases safely.

questions.prompt: Explain how direction vectors simplify neighbor exploration in grid problems like Depth-First Search and Breadth-First Search. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Direction vectors store coordinate offset pairs like (-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), and (0, -1) in a compact array. Instead of writing four repetitive if-blocks, you iterate over the vector array with a single clean loop. For each neighbor offset, you compute newRow and newCol, check bounds, and branch. This technique eliminates duplicated logic and reduces bugs.

rubric.criterion: Explains that direction vectors represent delta offsets (dr, dc) for adjacent cells.
Highlights that iterating over offsets replaces repetitive manual branching logic.
Mentions applying coordinate addition and bounds checking inside a unified loop.

questions.prompt: Describe the two-step algorithm to rotate an n by n square matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place with O(1) auxiliary space. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: The first step transposes the matrix across its main diagonal by swapping matrix[r][c] with matrix[c][r] for all c greater than r. This flips the rows into columns. The second step reverses each row horizontally. Performing these two transformations in sequence rotates the matrix 90 degrees clockwise while reusing the existing memory buffers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies step one as transposing the matrix across the main diagonal.
Identifies step two as reversing each row horizontally.
Explains that combining both steps achieves in-place rotation with O(1) auxiliary space.

questions.prompt: Compare Depth-First Search and Breadth-First Search for matrix grid problems, identifying when you would choose each approach. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Depth-First Search explores paths deeply using recursion or a stack. DFS is ideal for counting connected components, flood fill, and backtracking searches. Breadth-First Search explores outward layer by layer using a queue. BFS is ideal for finding the shortest path in an unweighted grid. The first time a target cell is reached, the path is shortest.

rubric.criterion: Describes DFS as depth-oriented traversal best suited for connected components or flood fill.
Describes BFS as level-oriented traversal best suited for shortest path queries.
Identifies that DFS relies on recursion/stacks while BFS uses an explicit queue.

questions.prompt: Explain why iterating row by row through a Swift [[Element]] matrix performs better than iterating column by column. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: A Swift matrix is an outer array containing references to independent row arrays. When iterating row by row, memory access is contiguous within each row buffer. This sequential pattern enables the CPU hardware prefetcher to load cache lines efficiently. Iterating column by column hops between separate row allocations, causing frequent CPU cache line misses and slowing down execution.

rubric.criterion: Explains that row-by-row traversal accesses contiguous memory within each row buffer.
Describes how contiguous access maximizes CPU cache hits and prefetching efficiency.
Notes that column-by-column traversal causes cache misses by jumping across separate buffers.
